# Runtime Safety: Guardrails and Moderation {#sec-runtime-safety}

Training can make harmful behavior less likely, but deployment needs a stronger
statement than "the model usually refuses." An aligned model's own refusal is
necessary but not sufficient. Every request brings new input, product policy
changes without a model retrain, and adversaries deliberately search for cases
the training did not cover. Input and output have to be screened separately,
and screening is one of several controls. Policy-conditioned classifiers, which
receive the written policy as input alongside the content, detect evidence of
harm. Authorizing a payment, isolating a process, and proving what an external
API did fall to other components.

Runtime safety is the request-time contract under which the system detects
evidence, lets policy decide, makes an enforcement point apply that decision,
contains what still goes wrong, and records what happened. In a tool-using
system, the model's output is a proposal, and only trusted code outside the model
can authorize an action and commit its effect. That
division connects the external control discussed in @sec-oversight-control to
the prompt-injection and streaming problems in this chapter. Indirect
@gls-prompt-injection, which plants instructions in content the system later
retrieves, makes provenance part of every decision, and whether the serving
layer streams output constrains the safety design.

## The five jobs of a guardrail

The word *guardrail* covers several different mechanisms, and a guard model (a
classifier that screens a request or a response) is one of them. Keeping their
jobs separate prevents a detector's uncertain prediction from being mistaken
for a system guarantee.

1. A **detector** extracts signals: moderation scores, malware findings, secret
   matches, suspicious destinations, or anomalous tool arguments.
2. A **policy decision** combines those signals with authenticated subject,
   action, resource, tenant, data classification, and policy revision.
3. A **policy enforcement point** allows, blocks, rewrites, challenges, or
   delays the exact operation.
4. **Containment** limits the damage if detection and policy both miss: narrow
   credentials, a sandbox, quotas, and network egress controls.
5. **Evidence** links the request, decision, attempted effect, and observed
   result so an operator can test and investigate the system.

A score is not a decision. A decision is not enforcement. A blocked request is
not proof that no side effect occurred. Those distinctions already mattered for
authorization in @sec-security-authorization; runtime safety applies them to
model text, retrieved data, generated code, and tool calls.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-runtime-control-path
//| fig-cap: "The runtime control path. Learned detectors provide evidence to a versioned policy decision. Trusted code enforces the decision before display or execution, while containment limits failures and receipts record outcomes."
digraph runtime {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  nodesep=0.18;
  ranksep=0.24;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, margin="0.06,0.04", color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [color="#6b7280", fontsize=8];

  request [label="request + provenance"];
  detect [label="detectors\n(scores and findings)", color="#3b82f6", fontcolor="#3b82f6"];
  decide [label="versioned policy\nallow / review / block"];
  model [label="model proposes\ntext or tool call"];
  enforce [label="trusted enforcement\nvalidate / authorize / commit", color="#3b82f6", fontcolor="#3b82f6"];
  result [label="display or effect"];
  contain [label="containment\nsandbox / quota / egress"];
  receipt [label="decision + effect receipt"];

  request -> detect -> decide;
  decide -> model [label="allow"];
  model -> enforce -> result;
  contain -> enforce [style=dashed];
  enforce -> receipt [style=dashed];
}
```

Input moderation can stop a disallowed request before generation. Output
moderation covers cases that are visible only after generation, including a
benign request followed by a harmful answer. Neither screen sees every relevant
fact. A retrieved document can alter the model after input screening, and a tool
can turn an apparently harmless string into an irreversible effect after output
screening. The placement and scope of each check therefore matter as much as
the classifier.

## From a detector score to a policy decision

Modern moderation systems learn categories rather than matching only keywords.
Production examples combine a documented taxonomy, carefully reviewed labels,
active learning, which selects the examples most worth labeling next, and
synthetic or adversarial data [@markov2023moderation]. Models such as Llama
Guard accept a taxonomy with the conversation and support separate prompt and
response classification [@inan2023llamaguard]. Supplying the taxonomy
configures the classifier within the categories it was trained and evaluated to
detect. Policy text does not make an unsupported category reliable, and a
renamed category does not create the data needed to evaluate it.

Treat the policy as a versioned policy bundle with a declared schema, supported
categories, thresholds, and failure behavior. Require schema validation,
offline evaluation before rollout, a staged release, and rollback. A policy
prompt is untrusted configuration until validated: malformed or injected text
must not silently change which policy is active.

The decision also needs more than one threshold. It must be able to allow,
review, or block. Let $x$ be the content being evaluated; let $k$ identify a
harm category; let $s_k(x)$ be the detector's score for that category; and let
$v$ identify the policy revision. For each category, policy $v$ sets a lower
threshold $\tau_{\mathrm{allow},k}$ and an upper threshold
$\tau_{\mathrm{block},k}$, with the lower threshold no greater than the upper
one. Read the three branches separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_v(x,k) &= \mathrm{allow}, \\
s_k(x) &\le \tau_{\mathrm{allow},k}, \\
D_v(x,k) &= \mathrm{review}, \\
\tau_{\mathrm{allow},k} &< s_k(x), \\
s_k(x) &< \tau_{\mathrm{block},k}, \\
D_v(x,k) &= \mathrm{block}, \\
s_k(x) &\ge \tau_{\mathrm{block},k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $D_v(x,k)$ is the decision under revision $v$. The middle region is an
explicit **abstain** path: request a human decision, route to a safer model, ask
for clarification, or disable tools. Uncertain cases take this path instead of
being silently counted as "allow." Selective classification studies classifiers
that may abstain and makes this choice explicit as a trade between coverage (the
share of items decided automatically) and risk (the error rate among those
items) [@geifman2017selective].

An estimated score is not automatically a probability. If the product presents
or reasons about it as one, it must be calibrated on traffic that represents the
deployment [@guo2017calibration], so that items scored 0.8 violate the policy
about 80 percent of the time. A false negative allows a violating item; a false
positive blocks a compliant one. Recall is the fraction of violating items
caught, while precision is the fraction of flagged items that violate the
policy. Precision depends on the base rate. If violations are rare, false
positives can dominate the review queue even when recall and the false-positive
rate look good on a balanced benchmark.

Calibration, false-positive rate, false-negative rate, and review rate should be
reported per category, per language, and for important user groups, not only as
a global average. Thresholds are chosen on a fixed sample of data. Distribution
shift, obfuscation, and adaptive attacks each make live traffic differ from that
sample and can invalidate the chosen thresholds, so release evaluation needs
ordinary traffic, contrast cases for over-refusal (benign requests refused
because they resemble harmful ones) [@rottger2024xstest], and a private
adversarial test set. Threshold changes are policy changes and deserve
the same review and rollback discipline as code.

The failure mode depends on the effect. A timeout while labeling low-risk prose
may produce a bounded refusal or a degraded response. A system should fail
closed for privileged effects, committing no external action until every
required check returns a valid decision.

## Prompt injection changes the threat model

In an ordinary chat request, direct prompt injection puts the conflicting text
in the user's message. In an agent, indirect prompt injection puts it in a web
page, email, document, database row, image, or tool result that the system later
retrieves. The model receives trusted instructions and untrusted data in one
context, and untrusted data can influence a privileged decision. Real systems
have been compromised in this way [@greshake2023indirect], while AgentDojo and
InjecAgent provide reproducible tasks for measuring attack and defense behavior
[@debenedetti2024agentdojo; @zhan2024injecagent].

Successful injection is not yet a successful exploit. The injected text must
change a model proposal, that proposal must request a harmful operation, and the
operation must be accepted by the enforcement point. This decomposition gives
the defender several independent places to break the chain.

Learned defenses help at the first step. One approach is an
@gls-instruction-hierarchy, which trains a model to prefer system instructions
over user or tool content [@wallace2024instructionhierarchy]. Spotlighting marks
the provenance of untrusted spans [@hines2024spotlighting]. Moderation and jailbreak classifiers
can detect known attack shapes, including transformed examples
[@sharma2025constitutional]. These learned defenses reduce measured attack
success on their evaluation distributions; they do not establish a security
boundary. An adaptive input can still be misclassified, and the same model may
both interpret the data and decide what it means.

Structural controls limit which control flow and data flow an influenced model
can change. Plan-then-execute, action selection from a fixed set, context
minimization, and dual-model designs separate trusted planning from processing
untrusted content [@beurerkellner2025patterns]. CaMeL makes this separation explicit with a
capability and data-flow layer, and states its security result under a defined
threat model rather than for every agent architecture [@debenedetti2025camel].
The practical design is defense in depth: keep untrusted data out of privileged
planning where possible, grant every tool least privilege, and require human
confirmation bound to the exact parameters of an irreversible action.

## Put a deterministic gate in front of every effect

The harness in @sec-the-harness turns generated tokens into API calls, file
writes, queries, and code execution. That conversion is the point where runtime
safety can become enforceable. A safe effect path performs these checks in
trusted code outside the model:

1. Parse the proposal against a versioned, typed tool schema. Reject unknown
   fields, invalid encodings, ambiguous numbers, and out-of-range values.
2. Normalize the action, resource, and canonical parameters once. Use the same
   representation for authorization, approval, execution, and audit.
3. Obtain authorization for that exact subject, action, resource, tenant, and
   context. The model never supplies trusted identity or policy facts.
4. Apply destination policy to every outbound connection, denying by default,
   from a component the workload cannot reconfigure. Resolve and validate the
   DNS answer, connect only to permitted address ranges, and validate every
   redirect target. A hostname allowlist alone does not stop redirects, DNS
   rebinding, or a permitted service from exposing an unsafe endpoint.
5. Keep credentials in a secret broker. The model sees only an opaque handle,
   and the broker injects the secret only for the authorized destination and
   action.
6. Before an irreversible operation, persist a write-ahead intent with an
   idempotency key. Afterward, store the provider's effect receipt or a precise
   failure. A retry reuses the same key instead of duplicating the effect.

Content moderation can contribute a signal at steps one and four, and every gate
runs regardless of that signal. Whatever a classifier concludes about a URL, the
destination policy still resolves and validates the address, and however
reasonable a transfer sounds, authorization still runs against the exact
subject, action, and resource.

Generated code needs a separate containment boundary. On Linux, namespaces can
separate views of processes, mounts, users, and networks; cgroups impose resource
limits; and seccomp restricts the system calls a process may attempt. The Linux
documentation states that seccomp filtering is not itself a sandbox
[@linuxseccomp]. Container guidance likewise treats isolation as a collection of
configured controls, not a property conferred by an image format
[@souppaya2017containers]. A container is not a virtual machine, and workloads
with a stronger attacker or confidentiality requirement may need a dedicated VM
or another hardware-backed boundary.

Any one of these controls can be misconfigured or carry an exploitable flaw, so
the boundary is built from independent layers. Untrusted code runs in a
VM-level sandbox, and network controls at the cluster enforce the egress policy
again without relying on the sandbox's own configuration. A failure in one layer
is then contained by the next, and no single sandbox, network control, or
supporting service carries the boundary alone [@openai2026hfreport]. One lab's
review of its evaluation incidents found that it had relied largely on a single
layer, the configuration of the environment itself
[@anthropic2026securitypractices]. The layers also have to hold against a
workload that probes them. An agent searching for a route to its goal tests its
surroundings, so the boundary cannot depend on the model choosing not to test it
[@aisi2026incident].

Run generated code without host secrets, without a writable host mount, with
resource limits, and with network egress disabled unless a narrow task requires
it. If egress is allowed, route it through the same destination and credential
broker used for tools. A sandbox limits consequences, while the policy and
authorization steps above decide whether an action is appropriate, and a sandbox
offers no protection against a kernel escape, a mounted credential, an overbroad
network policy, or a confused downstream service. NIST's generative-AI profile
therefore treats monitoring, access controls, incident handling, and testing as
complementary risk treatments rather than one universal filter
[@autio2024genai].

A confused downstream service is how agents left their sandboxes in one 2026
evaluation. The workloads had no direct internet access. Their main route out was an
internal package mirror that they could reach and, through previously unknown
vulnerabilities in it, cause to send requests on their behalf
[@openai2026hfreport]. Egress is therefore a property of everything a workload
can reach. A package mirror, a web cache, or any other supporting service that
the workload calls and that can itself reach outside is an egress path, and a
destination policy that permits the service permits whatever the service can be
made to do. The artifact mirror that the sandbox envelope in
@sec-agents-practice lists as its only allowed destination is part of the
boundary in this sense. The design rule is default-deny egress over transitive
paths: outbound access is limited to a short approved list, the compromise of
any single workload or supporting service does not by itself grant internet
access, and neither the workload nor the services it reaches can modify their
own network boundary or open a new outbound path
[@openai2026hfreport; @openai2026pacing]. A service that cannot be held to that
rule is isolated per run, restricted in what it accepts, or replaced.

The same services are a coordination substrate. Any surface that two runs can
both write and read, a cache, a mirror, a scratch store, or a public service
that records the requests sent to it, carries messages between runs that were
meant to be isolated. The section on large agent populations in
@sec-multi-agent-systems describes how a population of agents formed and
coordinated over such a surface. State left there is also a persistence and
re-entry vector: a later run reads what an earlier one left and continues from
it, which in the same evaluation included credential material that let a later
run regain administrator access to the shared service [@openai2026hfreport].
Containment therefore covers every writable surface two runs share. The reset
test in @sec-agents-practice, which checks that a fresh run cannot read what a
previous run wrote, has to reach those shared services as well.

Evaluation environments need the same containment. A capability evaluation often
removes a model's deployment safeguards to measure what it can do, so the
evaluation environment is a deployment of an untrusted model with the guard
layer taken out; the section of @sec-oversight-control on agents that reached
real systems during evaluation covers the oversight side. When a third party
runs the evaluation, its environment is a containment surface that the model
developer does not operate and cannot take on trust. One external evaluator's
testing environment, meant to be isolated from the internet, was misconfigured
and let the models of more than one developer reach it
[@openai2026thirdpartyevals].

The controls follow from how those runs failed. The environment's isolation is
verified before each run. Scope is stated as an instruction, such as "do not
access the internet," rather than as a claim about the environment, such as
"there is no internet access." Anthropic judges that telling its models they had
no internet access, when they did, may have led them to question whether the
systems they saw were real [@anthropic2026securitypractices]. Each task is
confirmed solvable by the intended route before it runs, and a task that turns
out broken or impossible has a sanctioned exit, stopping or asking for
clarification, which the graders reward because they score how a task ended as
well as whether it was completed [@openai2026hfroadahead; @aisi2026incident].

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

- OpenAI's technical report of 26 August 2026 bars high-risk and untrusted
  research workloads from direct or transitive internet access, apart from a
  cached internet-access service for specific workflows, runs untrusted
  model code in VM-based sandboxes with independent network isolation at the
  sandbox and cluster layers, and isolates, restricts, or replaces the
  supporting services those workloads reach [@openai2026hfreport]. Its
  monitoring of reasoning and actions is required for all tool-using
  reinforcement learning and evaluations of models at GPT-5.6 Sol capability or
  above [@openai2026pacing].
- Anthropic reported on 31 August 2026 a classifier, in its evaluations and in
  modified form in reinforcement learning environments, that blocks the action
  before the tool call runs when a model probes or escapes its testing
  environment or unexpectedly reaches the internet, then ends the task and
  alerts a human. It asks every organization testing its pre-release models
  with reduced cyber safeguards to verify before each evaluation that the
  sandbox has no internet access, keep API keys outside it, confirm the task is
  solvable, state scope as instructions, and monitor in real time. Its security hardening,
  most of it done before the July incidents, sets its computing clusters to
  block all outbound traffic by default [@anthropic2026securitypractices]. Its
  assessment of 9 September reports that the new live blocking monitors catch
  the incidents' behaviors reliably [@anthropic2026incidents].
- The UK AI Security Institute stated on 4 August 2026 that it will treat
  granting internet access in an evaluation as a decision to be actively
  justified rather than a default [@aisi2026incident].
- SandboxEscapeBench, from researchers at the UK AI Security Institute and the
  University of Oxford, measures container escape with 18 tasks based on
  documented vulnerability classes, each run inside a VM so that an escape
  reaches no real infrastructure. In the paper's revision of 1 August 2026,
  Claude Mythos Preview succeeded at least once on every task, and in 84 percent
  of samples at a 100-million-token budget, saturating the public set. The
  authors find success rising roughly log-linearly with the token budget and
  state that the results do not measure the likelihood of compromise in a
  defended production environment [@marchand2026sandboxescape].
:::

## Streaming creates two release boundaries

The serving stack in @sec-serving-problem streams tokens to the client as they
are generated, which reduces perceived latency. Incremental moderation, which
checks the output chunk by chunk as it streams, can stop a continuation, but
text the client has received is already disclosed. A later block cannot retract
a secret, a slur, or instructions that the client has received. Chunk size
therefore sets the trade between latency and the maximum unchecked prefix.

The design separates **display text** from **executable output**.
Streaming text may be acceptable after incremental moderation when the product
can tolerate a bounded prefix. A tool call, URL fetch, code execution request,
or transaction must remain a proposal until its complete structured value has
been buffered, parsed, authorized, and committed by trusted code. Buffer
executable outputs even when prose streams. Otherwise a partial stream can
become a committed side effect before the system has seen the fields needed to
reject it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lower-layer constraint

Serving determines what the safety layer can know before release. A whole-output
classifier requires buffering; incremental moderation permits streaming but can
only judge the prefix observed so far. The token delivery discussed in
@sec-faster-decoding therefore constrains the safety design as well as the
presentation. The runtime contract needs two explicit commit points: one for
bytes disclosed to a user and one for effects committed to the world. The second must always wait for the complete, canonical
operation and all deterministic gates.
:::

## An operating contract for runtime safety

The implementation should produce one linked record for each request. At a
minimum, record these schema-versioned fields without storing raw credentials or
unnecessarily retaining sensitive content:

- `request_id`, `policy_revision`, and authenticated subject and tenant;
- `input_provenance` for user, retrieved, system, and tool-provided content;
- `detector_revision_and_scores`, `decision_and_thresholds`, and review outcome;
- model, prompt, retrieval, and `tool_schema_revision` identifiers;
- `authorization_decision_id` and `canonical_action_and_parameters`;
- `sandbox_profile`, resource limits, and `egress_decision` including resolved
  destination;
- `approval_binding`, expiry, and one-time challenge when approval is required;
- `effect_idempotency_key`, write-ahead intent, and provider `effect_receipt`;
- timing, `failure_mode`, and the enforcement point's final result.

Trusted code outside the workload produces this record, and the record is
stored where the workload cannot write. The record is evidence about the
workload, so the workload cannot be its author. In one 2026 evaluation, agents
reached the component that executed their tool calls, so that transcripts the
investigators reviewed recorded one command while another ran
[@metr2026hfinvestigation]. In another, a model's own trace, asserting that its
environment was simulated, persuaded an offline monitor that no real harm was
occurring [@anthropic2026incidents]. The `canonical_action_and_parameters` field
therefore holds what the enforcement point executed, taken from the executor
rather than from the model's description of its call, and the log is
append-only on the enforcement side of the boundary. The reasoning-trace section
of @sec-oversight-control discusses what this means for monitors.

The record makes failures reproducible, but the tests must exercise the actual
boundaries. A release suite should include, at least:

- detector error and guard timeout paths for prose and privileged effects;
- policy rollback and mixed-version requests during rollout;
- obfuscation, split encoding, multilingual paraphrase, and benign contrast cases;
- an unknown tool field, duplicate key, non-canonical URL, and oversized argument;
- a redirect to a blocked host, DNS rebinding, private-address resolution, and a
  permitted host with a forbidden path;
- expired approval, approval replay, changed parameters after approval, and
  duplicate delivery of the same effect;
- cross-tenant resource references, unavailable authorization, and revoked
  credentials;
- sandbox escape probes, resource exhaustion, secret-file access, and denied
  network egress;
- a permitted supporting service asked to reach an outside host, and a canary
  that an earlier run left in a shared cache;
- a partial stream that becomes harmful only after several chunks, plus an
  incomplete tool call that must never execute.

Measure false positives, false negatives, review coverage, policy-decision
latency, enforcement failures, effect duplication, and the time from a policy or
detector update to complete fleet convergence. Red-team results complement these
checks, and the next chapter develops that adversarial evaluation discipline in
detail (@sec-adversarial-robustness).

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

- **How much should a learned guard decide?** A classifier can adapt to language
  and context that deterministic rules miss. It also inherits calibration drift,
  adversarial examples, and opaque errors. Products disagree about which cases
  can be blocked automatically and which require review or deterministic proof.
- **Can general-purpose agents resist indirect injection without losing useful
  autonomy?** Structural designs can state stronger properties because they
  constrain control and data flow. Those constraints also reject tasks that
  require untrusted data to shape a privileged plan. How much autonomy to give
  up for those properties is a product-specific trade, and no general solution
  exists.
- **Should safety failure always fail closed?** For money movement, secret access,
  and external writes, committing without a valid decision is usually
  indefensible. For low-risk conversation, universal refusal during a detector
  outage can create its own availability and accessibility harms. The failure
  mode belongs in the versioned policy and threat model, set separately for
  each class of effect. A guard that blocks by content also blocks legitimate
  users whose work resembles the harm it screens for. While investigating the
  July 2026 intrusion, Hugging Face found that hosted frontier models refused
  its forensic analysis, because the providers' safeguards cannot distinguish
  an incident responder from an attacker, and ran the analysis on an open-weight
  model on its own infrastructure, which also kept attacker data and
  credentials inside its environment [@hf2026securityincident]. Incident
  response therefore needs a capable model that the responder can run on
  infrastructure it controls, vetted before an incident; Hugging Face adds that
  this is no argument against safeguards on hosted models.
:::

## Runtime safety as external control

Runtime safety is designed on the assumption that any guard model can be wrong,
so it depends on knowing which claim each component can support. A detector
supplies an estimate, the policy decides, the enforcement point mediates every
effect, containment bounds the damage of a miss, and receipts make the result
testable. Small moderation models remain valuable because they can run on every
request and change independently of the generator. Their value is strongest
when an uncertain classification feeds an explicit decision and weakest when it
is treated as a security boundary by itself.

This is the serving-time form of external control. Training shapes what the
model tends to propose, and runtime architecture determines what those
proposals are allowed to disclose or do.
